stories.title: datasette-agent 0.3a0
stories.summary:
↳ WHAT'S NEW
datasette-agent 0.3a0 adds execute_write_sql — a new tool that lets the agent write to a Datasette database after requesting explicit user approval, with writes gated by Datasette's existing permission model.

↳ THE REAL STORY
Previous versions of datasette-agent were read-only: useful for querying and exploring data, but you couldn't close the loop and have the agent modify anything. execute_write_sql changes that. The approval step means the agent proposes the write operation, a human confirms, and only then does it execute — which is the right default for anything touching persistent state. Critically, it respects Datasette's existing permission layer, so you're not bypassing whatever access controls you've already configured.
stories.considerations: The interesting design question here is how much the approval UX actually protects you in practice. A human rubber-stamping AI-generated SQL at speed gets you most of the risk with little of the safety. The permission model integration is the more durable safeguard — but it's worth checking exactly which Datasette permission checks are being honored and whether there are edge cases around writable vs. immutable databases in your specific setup before trusting this in production.

stories.title: Frontier post-training recipe review with Finbarr Timbers
stories.summary:
↳ WHAT'S NEW
Interconnects published episode 18 of its interview series featuring Finbarr Timbers, covering a technical review of frontier post-training recipes — the RLHF, DPO, and fine-tuning pipelines that labs use to turn base models into deployed products.

↳ THE REAL STORY
Post-training is where most of the practical differentiation between frontier models actually happens, and detailed practitioner-level discussions of these pipelines are rare. A review of what's working at the frontier — reward modeling choices, data curation strategies, preference optimization variants — is directly applicable to anyone running their own alignment or fine-tuning work, even at smaller scale. The gap between what labs publish and what they actually do in post-training is wide; conversations like this narrow it slightly.
stories.considerations: The excerpt provided is essentially just a label — 'Interview #18' — with no substantive content to evaluate. Any specific claims about what Timbers covers, what recipes are discussed, or what conclusions are drawn would be fabricated from the title alone. Worth watching only after actually reading or listening to the full piece; the topic is genuinely important, but there is no signal here yet to assess.

stories.title: [AINews] Satya on Loopcraft: Building Frontier Ecosystems
stories.summary:
↳ WHAT'S NEW
Satya Nadella published an essay on what he calls "Loopcraft" — his framing for how frontier AI ecosystems get built, with Microsoft's stack as the implicit reference architecture.

↳ THE REAL STORY
The essay is less a product announcement and more a positioning document: Nadella is arguing that the next competitive moat isn't the model itself but the feedback loop infrastructure around it — data flywheels, agent orchestration, and enterprise integration layers. For developers, this is a signal about where Microsoft is placing its bets inside Azure and Copilot Studio. If your stack already leans on Azure OpenAI or Semantic Kernel, the direction Nadella is sketching — tighter loops between model outputs, user actions, and retraining signals — is where the platform investment is heading.
stories.considerations: The catch is that "ecosystem" essays from CEOs of platform companies are also competitive moats in disguise. Nadella framing the loop as the product is convenient when Microsoft controls the cloud, the IDE, the model API, and increasingly the agent runtime. Developers building on this stack should ask how much of their loop they actually own — and what the exit cost looks like if the platform terms shift. The essay is worth reading, but read it as strategy disclosure, not neutral architecture advice.

stories.title: The Fable 5 Export Controls Harm US Cyber Defense
stories.summary:
↳ WHAT'S NEW
Kate Moussouris (Luta Security) published a direct rebuttal to the framing that AI export controls strengthen US cyber defense — arguing the opposite. The piece addresses the specific "jailbreak" claim that circulated via The Atlantic.

↳ THE REAL STORY
The argument centers on a recurring policy blind spot: restricting AI model exports or access in the name of security can degrade the defensive security research ecosystem more than it limits adversaries. Moussouris, a credible voice in vulnerability disclosure and offensive security, is pushing back on the narrative that tighter AI controls equal better national cyber posture. For practitioners building security tooling or doing red-team work, this debate has direct implications — if export control logic gets applied to model weights or API access, the researchers who depend on open or accessible models for defensive work get squeezed first.
stories.considerations: The excerpt is too truncated to assess the full technical argument — specifically what the "jailbreak" claim actually was and whether Moussouris's rebuttal addresses it on the merits or primarily on policy framing. Simon Willison flagging that he should have gone to the source rather than The Atlantic's paraphrase is itself a signal: secondary sourcing on AI security claims is already distorting the policy conversation, and that distortion is happening fast enough that practitioners should read primary sources before the narrative hardens.

stories.title: Trump, Anthropic, Export Control, AI Race
stories.summary:
↳ WHAT'S NEW
The Atlantic reports Anthropic shared a White House report on the "Fable" jailbreak with external cybersecurity expert Katie Moussouris (CEO of Luta Security) for independent appraisal — part of broader coverage on Trump administration export controls and the US-China AI race.

↳ THE REAL STORY
The excerpt is too thin to reconstruct the full story, but the signal worth noting is the dynamic it reveals: Anthropic is actively seeking third-party validation of government security assessments tied to its models. If a jailbreak called "Fable" made it into a White House report, it suggests Claude's safety posture is now being evaluated at a policy level — not just by red teams inside the lab. For developers building on Claude, this means the regulatory surface area around the API is expanding. Export controls on frontier AI would directly affect who can access Claude-based products internationally.
stories.considerations:
↳ WORTH WATCHING
The unpaid, independent review framing is doing a lot of work here. Anthropic bringing in an outside expert to assess a government jailbreak report looks like responsible transparency — but it also functions as reputation management ahead of potential export control legislation. The open question: if the Fable jailbreak was serious enough to land in a White House report, what was the actual finding, and has it been patched? The excerpt doesn't say, and that gap matters more than the political theater around it.
